newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Draft EU treaty targets jobs, skirts UK minefield.
newsitem.headline: Draft EU treaty targets jobs, skirts UK minefield.

text.p: Ireland unveiled a draft new treaty for the European Union on Thursday which attacks crime and unemployment but skirts the minefields of voting rights and flexible integration which some states, notably Britain, would object to.

"All member states will see their positions reflected in the draft, but equally there will be very firm recommendations from the (Irish EU) presidency in the form of treaty language on the great bulk of the subject matter," Irish Prime Minister Joah Bruton tola a news conference.
The draft, which a senior Irish official said was "pitched at the upper end of realism", will be discussed by EU leaders at next week's summit in Dublin.

The product of bi-weekly meetings of the EU's inter- governmental conference (IGC) over the past five months, the draft carefully avoids the most contentious issues such as the right to veto legislation and "flexibility" about progress towards closer economic ties.

Britain, fearful of anything which smacks of surrendering more sovereignty to Brussels, is deeply suspicious of Franco-German plans to allow some countries to integrate their economies faster then others.
"Naturally during negotiations, everybody will be adopting a reserved position in regard to some matter or another," Bruton said in reply to a question about British opposition.

"But there is, I believe, clearly a will to negotiate because there is a recognition that if we are to have enlargement, you need to have reform. I think it's fair to say one of the countries that favours enlargement is the country you mentioned in your question," he added.

The draft, which was being rewritten in Dublin as late as Wednesday night, also studiously avoids potential rows by leaving out other areas of major disagreement such as the right of each country to have an EU Commissioner and extended qualified majority voting.
"We will not be producting a draft fait accompli so to speak on that subject at all. We will be giving a description on the difficulties," Bruton said.
"I believe that although we will not be producing a treaty draft, progress has been made in terms of better understanding of respective positions on that issue."

Ireland is one member state which opposes any change to the right of each member state to have an EU Commissioner, fearful that smaller states will lose out as the EU enlarges towards the East and South.

But the draft does address the major EU concern of unemployment by committing member states to co-ordinate their employment policies and to set objectives -- but not targets -- to get people back to work.
The draft, which is supposed to be ready for adoption at the next EU summit in the Netherlands next year, also attacks crime.
It proposes setting up an "area of freedom, security and justice" to align policies on immigration, visas and the rights of asylum seekers.
The draft promises to safeguard fundamental civil rights and to set a target date, possibly 2002, for new rules governing the EU's external borders and immigration.

It also seeks to co-ordinate the bloc's fight against the increasing use of and trafficking in illegal drugs and to attack crime. "It's a fairly ambitious proposal for a whole new section of the treaty," the diplomat said.
The EU ordered a revision of its treaties at a summit in June in Florence as part of its preparations for taking in a dozen new members from Eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.
